interactions.label: Cyclical bilateral mastalgia is a common presentation of early breast cancer.

params.question: Cyclical bilateral mastalgia is a common presentation of early breast cancer.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Cyclical bilateral mastalgia is common and usually benign. When breast pain tracks the menstrual cycle and affects both breasts, cancer is an unlikely cause. Malignancy-related pain, when present, is typically unilateral and non-cyclical.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Cyclical bilateral mastalgia is common and almost always benign — it reflects hormonal breast tissue changes, not malignancy. Cancer-related breast pain is rare and typically unilateral.

params.question: A 28-year-old woman presents with a painless breast lump. Following the triple assessment protocol, which imaging modality is the most appropriate first-line investigation?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Mammography is less effective in the dense breast tissue of younger women and is first-line only for patients over 35–40 years, when fatty replacement improves its sensitivity.
Correct. Under 35, breast tissue is dense, making ultrasound the first-line imaging modality. It effectively distinguishes solid from cystic lesions and is safe in pregnancy.
MRI is reserved for specific indications such as BRCA screening or evaluating disease extent, not routine first-line imaging of a breast lump.
PET-CT is used for staging advanced or metastatic disease, not for initial evaluation of a breast lump.

overallFeedback.feedback: Imaging in triple assessment follows age: under 35, the breast is dense, so ultrasound is first-line. Over 35–40, mammography becomes first-line as fatty replacement improves its sensitivity.
Correct — ultrasound is first-line for women under 35 because their dense breast tissue limits mammographic sensitivity.

params.question: Why does a phyllodes tumour require wide local excision with clear margins rather than simple enucleation?

answers.text: Phyllodes tumours invariably metastasise to axillary lymph nodes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Phyllodes tumours rarely metastasise via lymph nodes. The malignant variant may spread haematogenously, but lymph node involvement is not the concern driving wide excision.

answers.text: Enucleation cannot provide tissue for receptor status testing

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Receptor status (ER, PR, HER2) guides carcinoma treatment, not phyllodes management. Both procedures yield tissue for histological analysis.

answers.text: Phyllodes tumours can be borderline or malignant and recur locally if margins are incomplete

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Phyllodes tumours span a spectrum from benign to malignant. Incomplete excision risks local recurrence, so clear surgical margins are essential.

answers.text: Simple enucleation carries a higher risk of wound infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Infection risk depends on surgical technique and patient factors, not the type of excision. The reason for wide excision is oncological safety, not infection prevention.

overallFeedback.feedback: Phyllodes tumours can be benign, borderline, or malignant. Simple enucleation risks leaving tumour cells at the margin, leading to local recurrence. Wide local excision ensures adequate oncological clearance.
Correct — since phyllodes tumours range from benign to malignant, wide local excision with clear margins is essential to prevent local recurrence.

interactions.label: What is the principal clinical significance of lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)?

params.question: What is the principal clinical significance of lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS)?

answers.text: It serves mainly as a risk marker for future cancer in either breast

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. LCIS indicates an increased risk of developing invasive cancer in either breast, rather than being a direct precursor — distinguishing it from DCIS.

answers.text: It is a direct precursor that inevitably progresses to invasive lobular carcinoma

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Unlike DCIS, LCIS is not a direct precursor to invasive disease. It does not inevitably progress to cancer but signals elevated bilateral risk.

answers.text: It characteristically presents as microcalcifications on mammography

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Microcalcifications on mammography are the hallmark of DCIS, not LCIS. LCIS is typically an incidental histological finding.

answers.text: It is the commonest type of invasive breast cancer

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Invasive ductal carcinoma (no special type) is the commonest invasive breast cancer, accounting for 70–80% of cases. LCIS itself is not invasive.

overallFeedback.feedback: LCIS acts mainly as a risk marker — it signals elevated cancer risk in either breast. In contrast, DCIS is a premalignant lesion confined to ducts that can progress to invasive disease if untreated.
Correct — LCIS is a risk marker for future cancer in either breast, unlike DCIS which is a true premalignant lesion that can progress to invasive disease.

params.question: A core biopsy confirms invasive breast carcinoma in a 52-year-old woman. Using the SPIKES framework, what should the clinician do before delivering the diagnosis?

answers.text: Outline all surgical options and their survival statistics

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Treatment details follow the diagnosis and emotional response. Presenting them first overwhelms the patient before she has heard or processed the diagnosis.

answers.text: State the diagnosis immediately using precise medical terminology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: SPIKES advises delivering the diagnosis in plain language with a 'warning shot,' not abruptly in technical jargon.

answers.text: Ask the breast-care nurse to leave to ensure patient privacy

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The SPIKES framework recommends having a breast-care nurse present for emotional support during disclosure, not absent.

answers.text: Assess her perception of the situation and ask how much detail she wishes to hear

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The Perception and Invitation steps of SPIKES ensure you understand what the patient already suspects and how much information she is ready to receive, before delivering the diagnosis.

overallFeedback.feedback: Before delivering a cancer diagnosis, the SPIKES framework directs the clinician to assess the patient's existing perception and ask how much she wants to know, ensuring information is delivered at the right pace and depth.
Correct — assessing the patient's perception and inviting her to set the information depth are essential SPIKES steps before delivering the diagnosis.
